title: Exposure therapy for PTSD
description: Prolonged exposure is a trauma-focused therapy: over about ten weeks, people revisit the memory of the trauma in a safe setting and gradually face reminders they have been avoiding, so that the fear can fade. Studies scanned people before and after therapy, while recalling that a signal had become safe, and at rest. In the first part, dashed lines show links that were weaker than in trauma-exposed people without PTSD. After that, brightness and lines show the change since before treatment: warmer or a pulsing line means more than before, violet or a dashed line means less.
caveat: The findings come from two research groups. One group's two reports (16 and 24 people with PTSD) come from the same patients, compared with trauma-exposed people without PTSD but not with untreated patients. The other was a randomised trial against a waiting list, with about 50 people rescanned. Two reports measured how areas work together at rest, which is not the same as activity, and one measured activity while recalling that a signal had become safe. The rostral anterior cingulate is drawn on the pregenual cingulate, and the left frontoparietal "executive control" areas on the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex; both are approximations. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before therapy, the amygdala was less in step with the left orbitofrontal cortex, and the hippocampus with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, than in trauma-exposed people without PTSD.

phases.name: Ten weeks of exposure
phases.caption: About ten weekly sessions of revisiting the trauma memory and facing reminders. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.title: Neural changes in extinction recall following prolonged exposure treatment for PTSD: A longitudinal fMRI study.
citations.quote: The same procedures were repeated 10 weeks later, after PTSD patients had completed prolonged exposure treatment.

phases.name: Remembering safety
phases.caption: While recalling that a signal had become safe, the rostral anterior cingulate is less active than before therapy, and works more closely with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the subgenual cingulate.

citations.authors: Helpman L, Marin MF, Papini S, Zhu X, Sullivan GM, Schneier F, Neria M, et al.

phases.name: At rest
phases.caption: At rest, the weaker links are back to the level of people without PTSD, and the amygdala works more closely with the insula and less closely with left frontal "control" areas. Larger decreases in amygdala-frontal links went with larger improvements.

order.rationale: These come from scans at rest; they are shown after the task finding only to present one measurement at a time.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: Most of these studies did not compare therapy with untreated patients, so changes over time cannot all be credited to the therapy. These are small studies and not everyone improved.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.
